title: Data races
sub: Why count++ from two threads loses increments
cards/0/body: To the CPU, count++ is three steps: read count from memory, add 1, write it back. Remember CIL from the first unit? Here it is:
cards/0/code:
ldsfld  int32 Program::count   // read
ldc.i4.1
add                            // add
stsfld  int32 Program::count   // write
cards/1/task: Two threads do count++. Pick an order of steps so that count ends up equal to 1.
cards/2/q: Why did we get 1 and not 2?
cards/2/options/0: Both threads read 0 before anyone wrote 1
cards/2/options/1: The CPU can't add from two threads
cards/2/explain: Each added 1 to the 0 it had read and wrote 1. The second increment overwrote the first.
cards/3/task: Now for real: two threads each do count++ 1,000 times. Run it a few times and look at the results.
cards/4/q: Why is the result different every time and almost never 2,000?
cards/4/options/0: Thread switches land at different moments
cards/4/options/1: count++ has a random number generator inside
cards/4/explain: An increment is lost only when a switch happens between the read and the write. That happens more often on some runs, less on others.
cards/5/title: This is called a data race
cards/5/body:
A race condition is when the result depends on how threads happened to switch.

These are the nastiest bugs: everything works on the developer's machine, but on a loaded server it breaks once a week. The debugger often "cures" a race because it changes the timing.
cards/6/q: Where can a race happen? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/0: Two threads add items to the same List<T>
cards/6/options/1: Two threads do total += x on a shared field
cards/6/options/2: One thread checks if (cache == null) while another is filling it
cards/6/options/3: Each thread sums into its own local variable
cards/6/options/4: Two threads only read an immutable string
cards/6/explain: A race needs shared mutable memory and at least one write. Your own local variables and reading immutable data are safe.
cards/7/q: This method is called from many threads. Where is the race?
cards/7/explain: _hits is a shared static field, and ++ is three steps. local belongs to each thread separately.
cards/8/q: Two threads add to the same List<T> without synchronization. What can happen?
cards/8/options/0: Lost items or an exception: List<T> isn't thread-safe
cards/8/options/2: The items just end up shuffled
cards/8/explain: Add has several steps inside too: check the size, write, bump the counter. A race breaks them. That's what ConcurrentQueue, ConcurrentDictionary or lock are for.
